parts.text: What are 4 interventions from infection control?

cohort_answer.text: Cohorting of patient; Rapid diagnostics; Treatment; Droplet precautions; Airborne precautions for AGMPs; Prophylaxis.

Enhanced droplet/contact precautions for avian flu. Organizational controls: facility design (single rooms, accessibility to PPEs), policies and procedures, triage/screening/assessment. Patients with compatible symptoms and/or travel should be promptly placed in droplet contact precautions. Surveillance, laboratory testing/reporting. Respiratory hygiene, hand hygiene. Patient flow/activities restricted, management of visitors. Appropriate PPE - contact/droplet precautions. Education of healthcare personnel

parts.text: A. How viral infection predispose to bacterial infection

cohort_answer.text:
Numerous alterations of the respiratory epithelium and host immune responses occur during influenza virus infection that predisposes a host to coinfection with bacterial pathogens:
As influenza virus infects and kills host cells, epithelial surfaces become exposed and permissive to bacterial attachment.
Physical barriers (e.g., mucociliary transport) are damaged, pathogen detection is decreased
Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are downregulated, receptors are upregulated, virus production is enhanced, bacterial transepithelial migration is permitted, and repair mechanisms are lost.
Several host responses are also dampened, altered, or removed.
Alveolar macrophages, neutrophils, dendritic cells, and NK cells have altered cytokine profiles and become impaired and/or depleted. These changes result in a heightened inflammatory environment with decreased bacterial surveillance and eradication

Influenza causes desquamation or loss of ciliated columnar epithelium
Decreased pathogen detection
Reduced clearance of bacteria from epithelial surfaces

questions.question:
Q3 (2009 AM)
Indication for antivirals against influenza
Adult Risk Factors:

parts.text: Adult Risk Factors: (what are the indications/risk factors for antiviral treatment in adults)

Compare and contrast amantadine, oseltamivir, zanamivir with respect so mechanism, viral life cycle affected, side effect, whether sensitive or resistant to seasonal H1N1 non pandemic, H1N1 swine, H5N1 and H3N2

cohort_answer.text:
A - IDSA indications for treatment: Clinicians should start antiviral treatment as soon as possible for adults and children with documented or suspected influenza, irrespective of influenza vaccination history, who meet the following criteria: Persons of any age who are hospitalized with influenza, regardless of illness duration prior to hospitalization (A-II). Outpatients of any age with severe or progressive illness, regardless of illness duration (A-III). Outpatients who are at high risk of complications from influenza, including those with chronic medical conditions and immunocompromised patients (A-II). Children younger than 2 years and adults >=65 years (A-III). Pregnant women and those within 2 weeks postpartum (A-III). Clinicians can consider antiviral treatment for adults and children who are not at high risk of influenza complications, with documented or suspected influenza, irrespective of influenza vaccination history, who are either: Outpatients with illness onset <=2 days before presentation (C-I). Symptomatic outpatients who are household contacts of persons who are at high risk of developing complications from influenza, particularly those who are severely immunocompromised (C-III). Symptomatic healthcare providers who care for patients who are at high risk of developing complications from influenza, particularly those who are severely immunocompromised (C-III)

Adult Risk Factors list: Age >65, Chronic lung disease, CV/Renal/Liver disease, Hematologic, Metabolic condition, Immunosuppression, Neurological deficit/dementia, Obesity, LTC resident, Indigenous, pregnant

Pediatric Risk Factors (Last year's answer): Age <4 (especially if <2), Chronic medical conditions, Immunosuppression, Cognitive dysfunction/seizure/NM disorder, Long term ASA use (risk of Reye syndrome), Resident of CCC

Activity against H1N1 swine | Sensitive | Sensitive | Sensitive | sensitive. Activity against H5N1 | | | | Susceptible. Activity against H3N2 | Resistant | Resistant | | Susceptible

A. Describe/explain issues around influenza pandemic potential and avian influenza

cohort_answer.text:
Birds have all 16 HA subtypes and all 9 NA subtypes in their circulating influenza A viruses. Past pandemics resulted from novel reassortments of virus that passed from birds to humans, sometimes with other mammals as intermediaries. H9, H7, H5 variants have all been tracked to birds. Most transmission events seem to result in mild disease, small number of people affected and limited human to human transmission. More recent cases have been tracked directly to live bird markets (e.g. of H7N9) and felt to have limited inter-human transmissibility.
Avian strains prefer receptors with different sialic acid-galactose linkages than what is present in humans, therefore rare to have coinfection in humans -> Need third species, like a pig, with receptors for both strains where reassortment can occur. Also non-HA genes may mediate this restriction of hosts and replication further.
Avian strains can also adapt to human hosts through evolution in swine with multiple receptors, even without the presence of human virus (e.g. a drift mechanism).

questions.question:
Q6 (2003 AM)
3 cases of influenza, 2 of which are confirmed as influenza A in a hospital heme/onc ward.

parts.text: What are three methods of prophylaxis?
B. What are the advantages and disadvantages of each?

cohort_answer.text:
Part 1: Antiviral chemoprophylaxis - Preexposure: > 3mo and high risk group, give for the whole season. Post exposure e.g. PrEP and PEP, either to patients or to healthcare workers. In setting of outbreak on ward generally give for at least 2 weeks and one week after onset of last illness. If exposed and able to be vaccinated, vaccine can be given followed by PEP for 2 weeks if good match. Immunoprophylaxis - generally given as PrEP. (NOTES: PEP: Within 48 hrs and for 7 days only in outbreak settings and special situations.)

Part B: Chemoprophylaxis to patients - Advantages: Immediate effect, prevent spread to high risk patients. Disadvantages: Cost, patient side effects, not all patients eligible e.g. GI tract issues, Need to recognize outbreak before implementation. Can promote resistance.
Chemoprophylaxis to HCW - Advantages: Immediate effect, prevent spread to high risk patients as often mediated by healthcare workers moving from room to room; can limit sick days and presenteeism. Disadvantages: Cost, side effects, need to recognize outbreak before implementation, can promote resistance.
Immunoprophylaxis of patients and healthcare workers: Advantages: Can be implemented in advance to prevent outbreak; can cover non-outbreak strains; does not require on-going drug administration and less GI side effects. Disadvantages: Delayed effect of 2 weeks for full benefit, during which may contract illness, certain patients may have contraindications to vaccine, May be ineffective if weak immune system or poor match, Cost (cost effective for high risk patients but perhaps not for healthy adults), side effects

questions.question: AM 16. List of viruses - name whether it is DNA/RNA, Enveloped/not, and name an antiviral used for treatment (not immunotherapy) (whole chart - 3): Measles, Mumps, EBV, Zika, Ebola, Influenza, Hepatitis B (and Coronavirus)

cohort_answer.text: Measles - Paramyxoviridae, ssRNA(-), enveloped: nothing (ribavirin trialed in severe cases, vitamin A). Mumps - Paramyxoviridae, ssRNA(-), enveloped: nothing. EBV - Herpesviridae, dsDNA, enveloped: nothing (GCV, cidofovir tried). Zika - Flaviviridae, ssRNA(+), enveloped: nothing. Ebola - Filovirus, ssRNA(-), enveloped: remdesivir, or Ervebo vaccine. Influenza - Orthomyxoviridae, ssRNA(-), enveloped: Oseltamivir/zanamivir/baloxavir. Hepatitis B - Hepadnaviridae, partially ds/partly ss circular DNA, enveloped: tenofovir, lamivudine, entecavir. Chikungunya - Togaviridae, ssRNA(+), enveloped: no Rx. Coronavirus - positive sense ssRNA, enveloped with club-shaped spikes.
